name: Supervisor and Workers
question: Who splits the job and puts it back together?
summary: An orchestrator breaks a task into pieces and sends each to a worker sub-agent. Each worker starts with a fresh context, its own brief and a restricted set of tools, and returns only a short final message, so the orchestrator’s context stays clean. The orchestrator then merges the results and flags gaps. Anthropic calls this the orchestrator–workers pattern.
useCases: Research or review that splits into independent parts
Work where each part needs different tools or permissions
Long jobs where one context would overflow with raw material

items.detail: plans, delegates at run time and synthesizes
objective, output format, sources and task boundaries
a worker sees only its own prompt and the brief it is given
only the worker’s final message reaches the orchestrator
least privilege per worker, for example Read and Grep only
Claude Agent SDK: nesting depth 3 and 20 concurrent sub-agents by default

steps: Define each worker with a description, a system prompt and a minimal tool list
Write every brief so it carries all the context a fresh worker needs
Fan the workers out concurrently, with a budget or concurrency cap
Ask for a fixed, compact output format, then merge and list what is missing
pitfalls: Vague briefs make workers duplicate each other or wander out of scope
Returning full transcripts floods the orchestrator’s context
Spawning many workers for a simple question burns tokens for nothing
remember: Brief fully, scope tightly, return summaries.
caption: Illustrative: four workers each read about 30k tokens and return about 1k; the orchestrator holds 2k of its own plus 4k of summaries.

steps.title: Define the workers
steps.text: One sub-agent per drug class, each with a description (when to use it), a system prompt and a model.

steps.title: Restrict tools
steps.text: Screeners only read, so they get Read, Grep and Glob. A worker that cannot write cannot damage shared files.

steps.title: Write the brief
steps.text: A worker starts with a fresh context and sees only its own prompt, so the brief carries everything: objective, output format, sources and boundaries.

steps.title: Fan out
steps.text: The orchestrator calls the four workers through the Agent tool and they run at the same time, under one spend cap for the whole query.

steps.title: Collect summaries
steps.text: Each worker read about 30k tokens, but only its final message returns: about 1k each. The orchestrator holds about 6k, not 122k.

steps.title: Synthesize
steps.text: The orchestrator merges the rows, removes duplicates and lists what is missing, so a human reviewer sees both the findings and the gaps.

pros: The orchestrator decides the split at run time, so it adapts to each task
Workers’ raw reading stays out of the orchestrator’s context
Workers run in parallel and can use cheaper models
cons: The orchestrator is a single point of failure and a bottleneck
Vague briefs cause duplicated or out-of-scope work
Over-eager orchestrators spawn far more workers than needed
Summaries can drop details the merge step needed
avoidWhen: Steps are known in advance: a fixed graph is simpler and cheaper
A specialist should talk to the user directly: use a handoff instead

playgroundGuide.scenario: A pharmacovigilance orchestrator screens a week’s papers on 8 drug classes, about 240k tokens of reading. A quarter of the papers are only reachable by web fetch. Each worker’s window holds 100k tokens and reads about 10k tokens a minute; the orchestrator itself uses 2k tokens.

Choose how complete each worker’s brief is and which tools it gets.
Choose whether workers return a 1k structured summary or their full transcript.

presets.name: Better brief, transcripts back

presets.name: One worker

missions.hint: Give every worker the full brief: objective, output format, sources and boundaries.

missions.text: Reach 100% coverage without giving any worker write access.
missions.hint: At least 3 workers so the reading fits, the full brief, and read + web fetch tools.

tools.best: Sub-agents defined in code, each with its own prompt, tool list and model, called through the Agent tool.

practice.scenario: A Hyderabad pharma company’s pharmacovigilance team screens newly published papers every week for adverse events linked to its drugs. An orchestrator splits the screen by drug class and briefs one read-only worker per class. Each worker returns a structured summary, and a human safety reviewer checks the merged findings before anything is reported.

industries.use: One worker per drug or source, merged into one safety digest
Parallel checks on sanctions lists, adverse media and registries
Parallel code review: style, security and test-coverage workers

practice.analogy: A consultant partner and a team of analysts. The partner writes each analyst a clear brief, reads only their one-page memos, and writes the client report.

library.name: Claude Agent SDK
library.what: Defines sub-agents with their own prompt and tool list; the orchestrator calls them through the Agent tool and receives only each one’s final message.

practice.note: The depth and concurrency limits are environment variables; max_budget_usd caps the whole query, sub-agents included.

samples.code:
import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

CLASSES = ["SGLT2 inhibitors", "DPP-4 inhibitors", "statins", "ARBs"]
BRIEF = ("Screen papers in ./papers/{c} for adverse events. Objective: list every "
         "suspected adverse event linked to a {c} drug. Output: JSON list of "
         "{{drug, event, paper, quote}}. Use only the files given. Do not assess "
         "causality; stop when every file is read.")

agents = {
    c.split()[0].lower(): AgentDefinition(
        description=f"Adverse-event screener for {c}. Use for papers about {c}.",
        prompt=BRIEF.format(c=c),
        tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],          # read-only worker
        model="sonnet",
    ) for c in CLASSES
}

async def main():
    async for msg in query(
        prompt="Run every screener in parallel, then merge their JSON into one "
               "table and list any class with no papers read.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Agent"],
            agents=agents,
            env={"CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH": "1"},   # no nesting
            max_budget_usd=5.0,
        ),
    ):
        if hasattr(msg, "result"):
            print(msg.result)

asyncio.run(main())

numericDrill.question: An orchestrator uses 2k tokens of its own and sends out 6 workers. Each worker reads 25k tokens and returns a 1.5k summary. How many tokens does the orchestrator’s context hold after collecting summaries (in thousands)?
numericDrill.answer: 2k of its own + 6 × 1.5k of summaries = 11k tokens. If workers returned full transcripts it would hold 2k + 6 × 25k = 152k, which is why only final messages return.

interview.question: What must a worker’s brief contain, and why?
interview.answer: An objective, an output format, guidance on which tools and sources to use, and clear boundaries. The worker starts with a fresh context and sees only its own prompt and the brief, so anything missing is simply unknown to it.

interview.question: How is a supervisor different from a fixed execution graph?
interview.answer: In a graph the steps are fixed in advance by the developer. A supervisor decides at run time how to split the task, how many workers to start and what each should do, then merges what comes back.

mistakes.mistake: Don’t brief a worker with a one-line title.
mistakes.fix: Give it the objective, output format, sources and limits it needs.

mistakes.mistake: Don’t give every worker every tool.
mistakes.fix: Scope tools per worker: readers get read-only tools.

quiz.question: Four pharmacovigilance workers keep reading the same papers and returning overlapping findings. What is the most likely cause?
options: The workers use a small model
Their briefs lack clear boundaries: which drugs and sources each one owns
They return summaries instead of transcripts
The orchestrator merges too slowly
quiz.explanation: Without task boundaries each worker guesses its scope, so they overlap. A complete brief gives each one its own slice.

quiz.question: An orchestrator uses 3k tokens of its own and starts 5 workers. Each returns a 1.2k summary. How many tokens does the orchestrator hold after collecting them?
options: 6k
9k
3k

quiz.question: A compliance orchestrator briefs a sanctions-screening worker. What must the brief contain? Select all that apply.
options: The objective and the output format
The sources to use and where the task ends
The orchestrator’s full conversation so far
The other workers’ system prompts
quiz.explanation: A worker needs its objective, format, sources and boundaries. Passing the whole parent conversation or other workers’ prompts adds tokens without helping it.

quiz.question: In the Claude Agent SDK, what does a (non-fork) sub-agent receive from its parent?
options: The parent’s entire conversation history
Only the Agent tool’s prompt string, plus its own system prompt and tools
The parent’s system prompt and tool results
Nothing until it asks for context
quiz.explanation: The only content passed from parent to sub-agent is the Agent tool’s prompt, so it must carry whatever the sub-agent needs.

quiz.question: Four workers each read about 30k tokens. The orchestrator uses 2k of its own. If workers return 1k summaries instead of full transcripts, how many tokens stay out of the orchestrator’s context?
options: 6k
quiz.explanation: Transcripts: 2k + 4 × 30k = 122k. Summaries: 2k + 4 × 1k = 6k. Difference: 116k.

quiz.question: A code-review orchestrator starts style, security and test-coverage workers. None of them should change files. Which tool list fits the reviewers?
options: Read, Grep and Glob
Read, Edit, Write and Bash
All tools, since they may need one
No tools at all
quiz.explanation: Least privilege: reviewers need to read and search, not edit or run commands.

quiz.question: A shopping assistant’s orchestrator started 50 workers for “Which phone has the best camera under INR 30,000?”. What likely allowed this? Select all that apply.
options: No guidance on how much effort a query deserves
No cap on concurrency or spend
A vague objective in the orchestrator’s instructions
Workers returning short summaries
quiz.explanation: Anthropic saw early orchestrators spawn 50 sub-agents for simple queries. Effort guidance, clear objectives and caps prevent it; summaries are not the cause.

quiz.question: With the Claude Agent SDK defaults, how many sub-agents can run at once before new spawns are refused?
quiz.explanation: The default concurrency limit is 20; it can be lowered with CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS.

quiz.question: A LangGraph team is choosing how to build a supervisor. What does LangChain currently recommend?
options: The langgraph-supervisor library for all new projects
Building the supervisor directly with tool calling
A swarm of peer agents instead
CrewAI inside LangGraph
quiz.explanation: LangChain’s reference notes that it now recommends supervisors built with tool calling rather than the langgraph-supervisor library.

quiz.question: Six workers each read 40k tokens at about 10k tokens a minute, then the orchestrator merges for 1 minute. What is the wall time?
options: 24 minutes
5 minutes
4 minutes
25 minutes
quiz.explanation: Each worker takes 40k ÷ 10k = 4 minutes in parallel, plus 1 minute to merge = 5 minutes.

quiz.question: How does a supervisor differ from a fixed execution graph? Select all that apply.
options: A supervisor decides how to split the task at run time
A graph fixes its steps in advance
A supervisor cannot run workers in parallel
A graph cannot call language models
quiz.explanation: The difference is who decides the steps and when. Both can run work in parallel and both can call models.

quiz.question: Where should the human safety reviewer sit in a pharmacovigilance screen run by an orchestrator and workers?
options: Before each worker starts, approving its brief
After synthesis, checking the merged findings and listed gaps
Nowhere: the orchestrator is the check
Inside every worker, reading each paper
quiz.explanation: Reviewing the merged findings, including what could not be read, puts human judgement where it adds most at the lowest cost.

quiz.question: A legal research team has four reading workers and one that files the final memo into the matter folder. How should write access be granted?
options: To all five, for simplicity
Only to the filing worker, and only for its output location
To none; the orchestrator writes instead of the filing worker
To the reading workers only
quiz.explanation: Least privilege per agent: only the worker that must write gets write access, scoped to where it writes.

quiz.question: A research query with Claude sub-agents reaches its max_budget_usd. What happens?
options: The SDK silently raises the budget
New sub-agents are refused and the query ends with a budget error result
Only the orchestrator stops; workers carry on
Nothing until the next query
quiz.explanation: At the cap the SDK refuses further sub-agents, stops background ones and ends the query with the error_max_budget_usd subtype.

quiz.question: A network-operations orchestrator struggles to merge its workers’ results. Which output rules help? Select all that apply.
options: A fixed JSON schema for every worker’s return
A length limit on each return
Free-form prose so nothing is lost
The full transcript attached to every return
quiz.explanation: A fixed, compact format makes results comparable and keeps the orchestrator’s context small. Prose and transcripts make merging harder.

quiz.question: Four workers read 240k tokens in total, and 25% of that reading is duplicated because their scopes overlap. How many tokens are wasted?
quiz.explanation: 25% of 240k = 60k tokens spent reading what another worker already read.

quiz.question: A team studies Magentic-One’s orchestrator. What does it keep to plan and track progress?
options: A task ledger and a progress ledger
A vote among its workers
A single system prompt with no state
A handoff chain
quiz.explanation: Magentic-One’s orchestrator maintains a task ledger (facts, guesses, plan) and a progress ledger, and replans when progress stalls.

quiz.question: Claims arrive with different mixes of documents, so the subtasks are not known until the claim is read. Which Anthropic pattern fits?
options: Prompt chaining with fixed steps
Orchestrator–workers, where a central model breaks down the task and delegates at run time
Parallelization with a fixed set of sections
A single routing step
quiz.explanation: Anthropic describes orchestrator–workers as a central LLM that dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates them and synthesizes results.

quiz.question: You are designing a supervisor for a hospital’s research team. Which choices apply least privilege and bounded growth? Select all that apply.
options: Research workers get read-only tools
Only the report worker can write, to the report folder
Sub-agent nesting depth is capped
Every worker gets shell access in case it needs to install tools
quiz.explanation: Read-only readers, one scoped writer and a depth cap keep the team safe and bounded. Blanket shell access is the opposite of least privilege.

quiz.question: A logistics team sets CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH to 1. What changes?
options: Only one sub-agent can run at a time
Sub-agents cannot spawn sub-agents of their own
The orchestrator cannot spawn any sub-agents
Each sub-agent may use only one tool
quiz.explanation: Depth 1 stops sub-agents from spawning further layers; concurrency is a separate limit.
